title: Lead, kindly light
hookLine: John Henry Newman, stuck on a windless sea, writes a poem that asks for one step at a time

lines: A SICK MAN WANTS TO GO HOME.
cards: No wind. A sailing boat sits on flat water between Corsica and Sardinia, going nowhere.

On board is an English clergyman named John Henry Newman, weak from a fever he caught in Sicily, aching to get home, and unable to move. You can't argue with a calm sea, and you can't row a sailing boat home.
You can only wait. So, by the story Newman himself told, he writes a short poem. It's honest about the dark, and it asks for surprisingly little.
Later it became a hymn. Today's word is its first word, and it's a request.

teach.b: The poem opens: "Lead, Kindly Light, amid the encircling gloom, Lead Thou me on!" He doesn't ask for the wind, or a map.
Then the line the poem leans on: "Keep Thou my feet; I do not ask to see The distant scene; one step enough for me."

teach.h: I LOVED TO CHOOSE AND SEE MY PATH.
teach.b: Turn it one way, and it's a confession, from the next verse: "I loved to choose and see my path; but now Lead Thou me on!" A man who liked to plan, stuck on a sea that won't take orders.
Turn it another way, and it's very old.

teach.h: A PILLAR OF CLOUD BY DAY.
teach.b: Newman called the poem The Pillar of the Cloud, pointing back to Exodus, where the King James Bible says "the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light."
Israel in the wilderness never saw the whole route either; they followed the cloud.
Turn it a third way, and it sounds like a psalm: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet." A lamp at night lights the ground right in front of you, and almost nothing beyond.
Enough to walk. And a fourth way: his own life. The path Newman couldn't see took him somewhere he never planned.
Years later he left the Church of England and became a Catholic, which cost him friends, and the Catholic Church later named him a saint. Anglicans and Catholics both claim parts of his story.
The poem stays the same: one step, then the next.

how: Newman's poem is sung as the hymn Lead, Kindly Light in some English-speaking churches, and Christians in hard seasons sometimes pray its lines when they can't see what comes next.

o: a request: go ahead of me, and I'll follow
a heavy gray metal once used for church roofs
a command to take charge and guide others

games.q: lead, kindly light — tap the pairs.
p: what Newman does not ask to see

s: Newman asks to see the whole road ahead
he says the opposite: "I do not ask to see the distant scene."
Newman called the poem the pillar of the cloud
the title points back to Exodus, where God goes before Israel in a cloud by day and fire by night.
the poem says he always trusted the way he was led
he admits, "I loved to choose and see my path; but now lead Thou me on!"

games.q: you're on a boat that can't move, sick, far from home, with no idea when the wind will come. what do you do?
o: plan the whole journey home in detail.
write a poem asking only to be led one step at a time.
give up on getting home at all.
games.why: by Newman's own account, he wrote the poem: "I do not ask to see the distant scene; one step enough for me." the man who loved to plan asked for less.

practice: Set down the worries about how things turn out, next month, next year, the end of the road, one at a time, like heavy bags: the distant scene.

Then look only at the next hour and what it asks, maybe something small: a glass of water, a reply, a rest. If you pray, borrow Newman's words, lead Thou me on; if not, let that small thing be enough.

wordCard.voice: Lead. The first word of Newman's poem, a request from someone who can't see the way: go ahead of me, and I'll follow.

orig.note: Hebrew: lamp, the word in Psalm 119:105, thy word is a lamp unto my feet.

carryVoice: Your line: one step enough. Nobody has to see the whole road to walk it. Day nine hundred twenty-seven, done.
